posts.title: Why Hikari has no notifications
posts.excerpt: A planner that interrupts you is a planner that plans your day for you. We chose silence, and here is what it cost us.
posts.content:
When we started Hikari we wrote one rule on the wall: the app never speaks first. No pings, no badges, no red dots.

It cost us. Every growth guide says notifications bring people back. They do. They also teach people to open an app because it asked, not because the hour began.

Three years later, Hikari teams open the app about four times a day. That is the number we are proudest of.

posts.title: Quiet hours for the whole team
posts.excerpt: Version 3.2 lets a team protect the same two hours every day. A short note on how it works and why we built it.
posts.content:
Quiet hours used to be personal. You could protect your own afternoon, but a colleague could still pull you out of it.

From version 3.2 a team can share its quiet hours. During them Hikari dims softly, holds every message and shows only today.

Teams that tried it in the beta moved an average of two meetings out of the afternoon. Nobody asked them to.

posts.title: Three things, not ten
posts.excerpt: Why the week board stops at three things each, and what happens to everything else.
posts.content:
A list of ten is a list of wishes. A list of three is a plan.

The week board lets each person place three things on Monday. The rest go into a quiet drawer that nobody sees unless they open it.

It feels strict for a week. After that, most teams tell us the drawer is where things go to be honestly forgotten.

posts.title: The ten-minute Friday review
posts.excerpt: Three questions, the same every week. How a short written review replaced our longest meeting.
posts.content:
What moved? What stuck? What can wait? We ask the same three questions every Friday, in writing, together.

Writing is slower than talking, which is the point. A sentence has to be chosen; a meeting can drift for an hour.

The reviews are kept for a year. Reading last spring’s on a quiet Friday is the best planning we do.

posts.title: A paper warehouse in Kuramae
posts.excerpt: Our studio moved into an old paper warehouse by the river. A few notes on light, desks and working quietly together.
posts.content:
The building stored washi for sixty years. The walls still smell faintly of it on wet days.

We kept the long tables and the paper lamps, and added nothing that blinks. The only screen on the wall is a clock.

Visitors are welcome on Thursday afternoons. Write first, and we will make tea.

posts.title: Working across two time zones
posts.excerpt: Half of Hikari Labs is in Tokyo, a few of us are in Lisbon. How a quiet tool helps a split team overlap without overworking.
posts.content:
Tokyo and Lisbon overlap for about two hours a day. We protect those hours for talking and keep the rest for work.

The week board does most of the coordination. By the time Lisbon wakes up, Tokyo’s day is already written down.

It works because nobody expects an answer at once. Quiet is a kind of trust.
